title: Slide 1 · Explaining and testing a hybrid decision
question: A desk forwards a request when the photo score is at least 0.80 and the camera is available. The score is 0.93 and the inventory says unavailable. What would the rule do?
answer: It would hold the request. Both conditions must hold, and the inventory condition fails even though the score passes.

title: Slide 2 · What made this request reach the clerk?
question: Would “the model rejected the photo” explain why this request was held?
answer: No. The photo passed its cutoff. Inventory row I3 marked C1 unavailable, which made the final test fail. This trace explains the system’s behavior even if I3 later turns out to contain an error.

title: Slide 3 · Give the test a reference answer
question: Can the desk claim that this baseline successfully sends eligible requests to the clerk?
answer: It earns four correct holds but sends none of the two eligible requests. Overall accuracy hides that failure.

title: Slide 4 · Which part of the system helped?
question: Which row changes when inventory is added, and do the four hybrid agreements settle which system is best?
answer: Only R2 changes, from an incorrect send to a correct hold. Hybrid and always-hold both agree four times. The hybrid sends eligible R1 and ineligible R5, so the choice also depends on the costs of a missed request and an unnecessary review.

title: Slide 5 · Diagnose the two kinds of mistakes
question: What would you inspect before raising the cutoff to remove R5?
answer: Inspect the photos, their reference labels and their scores. R5 is an incorrect match at 0.85, but R4 is a real match at only 0.60. Raising the cutoff cannot recover R4. Choose changes on development cases, then evaluate on fresh held-out cases.

title: Slide 6 · Put each send in the right comparison set
question: Replace this line: sent = {"R1", "R5"} with: sent = {"R1", "R4", "R5"} What will print?
answer:
unnecessary review: ['R5']
missed: []
precision: 0.6666666666666666
recall: 1.0
R1 and R4 are both caught, so recall reaches 2/2. R5 is still an unnecessary review, which leaves precision at 2/3.

title: Slide 8 · From this module to the next
question: A teaching-room audit will screen staff notes and compare a check time with a handoff time. If one ticket is labeled incorrectly, what should you save so someone can tell which step went wrong?
answer: Keep the ticket ID, original note and its score, the handoff record, both event times and the rule used. A reviewer can then test whether the note was interpreted correctly and replay the time comparison independently.

title: Office hours · Can an explanation be faithful even when the decision is wrong?
question: Can an explanation be faithful even when the decision is wrong?
answer: Yes. A trace that says “I3 showed unavailable” can faithfully describe the program’s decision. If I3 was stale, that same trace helps a clerk find the problem. To judge correctness, compare the inputs and decision with independent evidence.

title: Office hours · Should I always choose the method with the highest accuracy?
question: Should I always choose the method with the highest accuracy?
answer: Ask what happens to each type of request. A desk that holds everything scores well when most requests should be held, but misses every eligible borrower. Count missed requests and unnecessary reviews, and relate both to the desk’s purpose.

title: Exercise 1
question: On ten reviewed requests, eight should be held. How accurate is always-hold, and what is its recall for eligible requests?
answer: It agrees eight times out of ten, or 80%. It sends zero of the two eligible requests, giving 0% recall. Precision for sends has a zero denominator here.

title: Exercise 2
question: The hybrid and the score-only method give the same wrong answer for R20. What evidence could distinguish a bad photo score from a bad inventory record?
answer: Compare the photo with the correct item and obtain an independently checked inventory snapshot at the request time. Replay both tests with those values. The failed comparison locates a possible error, and both components could be wrong.

title: Exercise 3
question: A team tries 20 score cutoffs on its final test set and reports the one that sent the most eligible requests with few incorrect sends. How would you redesign that evaluation?
answer: Choose the cutoff on a development set. Fix the threshold, inventory rule and evaluation measures, then run the comparison once on new held-out requests. Keep repeated copies of the same request together when dividing the data.

title: Lab case 1 · Trace one send
question: Write the explanation the clerk should see.
answer: P12 reaches the inclusive 0.80 cutoff and I12 lists C1 as available, so R12 is sent for review. Whether the photo really matches still depends on checking the source.

title: Lab case 2 · Identify a faulty record
question: Which component should you inspect first?
answer: The photo decision agrees with the independent check. The availability input disagrees. Inspect the inventory record, its timestamp and how R13 was linked to it.

title: Lab case 3 · Count two denominators
question: Calculate precision and recall.
answer: Precision is 2 of 3 sent requests. Recall is 2 of 4 eligible requests. One unnecessary review reduces precision and two missed eligible requests reduce recall.

title: Module overview · Explaining and testing a hybrid decision
question: What is this module about?
answer: Explaining and testing a hybrid decision. Trace a screening decision, compare a learned model and a rule on the same held-out requests, and locate an error using independent evidence.
